newsitem.title: GERMANY: German insurers opt for commitee on genetic tests.
newsitem.headline: German insurers opt for commitee on genetic tests.

text.p: German insurers are to set up an expert committee to evaluate the issue of genetic testing in insurance, leading representatives of the German insurance industry said.

Peter Greisler, chairman of the private health insurers' association PKV-Verband, told Reuters that such a motion would be discussed this week by the Committee of the German insurance association, Gesamtverband der Deutschen Versicherungswirtschaft.
So far, German insurers have not had a uniform view on genetic testing in relation to life and private health insurance, said Greisler.

Such tests can detect at an early age the possibility of a person developing certain diseases, including cancer. It was unclear at present what would happen to the results of genetic tests carried out for medical purposes, industry representatives said.
"In my opinion, it would not constitute a breach of obligation on the part of the applicant if he did not tell us of such test results," said PKV director general Dr Christoph Uleer.
In the UK, some insurers are seeking a framework under which they can routinely ask applicants for life or health cover to undergo a test.
In Austria, a law bans insurers from using any information gained by genetic tests, even if an applicant gives details.
In Switzerland, insurers have agreed voluntarily not to use such information, but have limited that to the period up to 2000.
"I cannot imagine such a voluntary restraint for Germany. We would immediately have competitors from other EU countries in our markets, who do not have such restrictions," Uleer said.
